'''''Rosa rugosa''''' ('''rugosa rose''', '''beach rose''', '''Japanese rose''', '''Ramanas rose''', or '''letchberry''') is a species of [[rose]] native to eastern [[Asia]], in northeastern [[China]], [[Japan]], [[Korea]] and southeastern [[Siberia]], where it grows on beach [[coasts]], often on [[sand]] [[dune]]s.<ref name=FOC>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200011310|title=''Flora of China''|publisher=eFlora|access-date=15 October 2011}}</ref> It is naturalized in much of [[Europe]] and parts of the United States and Canada.<ref name=POWO_927373-1>{{Cite POWO|title=''Rosa rugosa'' Thunb..|id=927373-1|access-date=2024-09-27|mode=cs1}}</ref> It should not be confused with ''[[Rosa multiflora]]'', which is also known as "Japanese rose". The Latin word "rugosa" means  "wrinkled", referring to the wrinkled leaves.<ref name=Jo>Jo Ann Gardner {{google books|ZG5UAwAAQBAJ|Living with Herbs: A Treasury of Useful Plants for the Home and Garden ...|page=220}}</ref><ref name=Sara>Sara Williams {{google books|V1GhisAjJm4C|Creating the Prairie Xeriscape|page=156}}</ref> Often used as an [[ornamental plant]], it has become [[Invasive species|invasive]] in parts of Europe, North America and South America.<ref name=CABI/><ref name=Breed2004/>

==Description==
''Rosa rugosa'' is a [[Basal_shoot|suckering]] [[shrub]] which develops new plants from the roots and forms dense thickets 1–1.50 m tall with stems densely covered in numerous short, straight [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|prickles]] 3–10 mm long. The [[leaf|leaves]] are 8–15 cm long, [[leaf shape|pinnate]] with 5–9 leaflets, most often 7, each leaflet 3–4 cm long, with a distinctly corrugated (rugose, hence the species' name) surface. The leaf is elliptical in shape with a rounded base or broadly cuneate with a leather feel, dark green top. The back of the leaf is composed of a green-grey colour with hair along the veins. The leaf margin is composed of teeth along the edges and is crenate-serrate. The flower has five petals that are usually 6–9 cm in width. The flower is composed of 200–250 stamens per flow and vary in style.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/Rosa-Rugosa-Rugosa-Rose|title=Rosa rugosa (Rugosa Rose)|website=Gardenia.net|language=en|access-date=2019-04-06}}</ref> The [[flower]]s are pleasantly scented; range in color from dark pink to white (on ''R. rugosa'' f. ''alba'' <small>(Ware) Rehder</small>), 6–9 cm across, with somewhat wrinkled petals; flowering occurs in spring.<ref name=FOC/>

The edible [[rose hip|hips]], which resemble cherry tomatoes, are large, 2–3 cm diameter, and often shorter than their diameter, not elongated. In late summer and early autumn, the plants often bear fruit and flowers at the same time. The leaves typically turn bright yellow before falling in autumn.{{Citation needed|date=July 2011}}

==History==
This rose species was introduced to America from Japan in the mid-19th century; it was valued both for its flowers and ability to resist beach erosion<ref name="Weidema-2006"/> because it can tolerate [[salt water]] spray.<ref name=Jo/>

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Rosa rugosa (55026907680).jpg|thumb|''Rosa rugosa'' near [[Frederikshavn]], Denmark during winter, 2025]]
''Rosa rugosa'' is widely used as an [[ornamental plant]]. It has been introduced to numerous areas of [[Europe]] and [[North America]]. It has many common names, several of which refer to the fruit's resemblance to a [[tomato]], including ''beach tomato'' or ''sea tomato''; others include ''saltspray rose'', and ''Turkestan rose''.<ref name=CABI>{{cite journal|last1=Pasiecznik |first1=Nick |title=''Rosa rugosa''|url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.1079/cabicompendium.47835|publisher=[[CAB International]] |journal=Invasive Species Compendium|date=2009 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.47835 |access-date=17 September 2014|doi-access=free }}</ref> In parts of the US, the fruits are also occasionally called ''beach plums'', causing confusion with the actual beach plum, ''[[Prunus maritima]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.capecodartandnature.com/2015/09/01/beach-rose-hips-are-not-beach-plums-and-other-things/|title=Beach rose hips are NOT beach plums and other things {{!}} Mary Richmond's Cape Cod Art and Nature|website=www.capecodartandnature.com|date=September 2015 |language=en-US|access-date=2017-12-25}}</ref>

The sweetly scented flowers are traditionally used to make flower [[jam]] and [[dessert]] in China.{{cn|date=August 2025}} They are also used to make [[Potpourri|pot-pourri]] in Japan and China. It is used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]].<ref name=TCMWiki>{{cite web|title=Mei gui hua|url=https://tcmwiki.com/wiki/mei-gui-hua|publisher=TCM Wiki|access-date=5 February 2017}}</ref> Beach [[rose hips]], like those of other rose species, are edible and can be used to make jams, syrups, tea, or eaten raw. <ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.edc.uri.edu/restoration/html/gallery/plants/rose.htm|title=Beach rose (Rosa rugosa)|website=www.edc.uri.edu|language=en-US|access-date=2021-07-23|archive-date=2022-09-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220920172527/http://www.edc.uri.edu/restoration/html/gallery/plants/rose.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

This species [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridises]] readily with many other roses,<ref name=CABI /> and is valued by rose [[Plant breeding|breeders]] for its considerable resistance to the diseases [[rose rust]] and [[rose black spot]]. It is also extremely tolerant of seaside [[sodium chloride|salt]] spray and [[storm]]s, commonly being the first shrub in from the coast. It is widely used in [[landscape design|landscaping]], being relatively tough and trouble-free. Needing little maintenance due to its being very disease resistant, it is suitable for planting in large numbers; its salt-tolerance makes it useful for planting beside roads which need [[deicing#Roads|deicing]] with salt regularly.<ref name=nobanis/> It can control erosion.<ref name="Weidema-2006">{{Cite web|title=Invasive Alien Species Fact Sheet –Rosa rugosa|last=Weidema|first=I|date=2006|url=https://www.nobanis.org/globalassets/speciesinfo/r/rosa-rugosa/rosa_rugosa.pdf|publisher=Agency for Spatial and Environmental Planning, Ministry of the Environment, Copenhagen, Denmark}}</ref>

Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been selected for garden use, with flower colour varying from white to dark red-purple, and with semi-double to double flowers where some or all of the [[stamen]]s are replaced by extra petals. Popular examples include 'Rubra Plena' (semi-double variant, with strong clove scented dark pink petals and dark green wrinkled leaves and large round orange-red hips),<ref name=Jo/> 'Hansa' (fragrant, red-purple double),<ref name=Sara/> 'Fru Dagmar Hastrup' (pink, single), 'Pink Grootendorst' (pink, semi-double), 'Blanc Double de Coubert' (white, double) and the more common 'Roseraie de L'Haÿ' (pink, double),<ref>{{cite web |title=ROSE, ROSERAIE DE L'HAY (Rosa rugosa Roseraie de L'Hay). Hedging Plants, Trees, Shrubs and Conifers. |url=https://www.hedging.co.uk/acatalog/product_10293.html |website=www.hedging.co.uk |access-date=29 October 2019}}</ref> which is often used for its very successful rootstock and its ornamental rose hips.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rugosa Roses - Shrub Roses - Type |url=https://www.davidaustinroses.co.uk/type/shrub-roses/rugosa-roses |website=www.davidaustinroses.co.uk |access-date=29 October 2019}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
[[File:Rosa rugosa plant (08).jpg|thumb|Dense thicket of ''R. rugosa'' in coastal [[New England]], United States]]

In its native China, ''Rosa rugosa'' has been labeled as an endangered species due to a noticeable high decline in population rates of the flower, but in other continents where [[Introduced species|introduced]] it has become naturalized and is considered [[Invasive species|invasive]].<ref name=Breed2004/> It can outcompete native flora and form dense thickets that completely cover large areas, thereby threatening biological diversity.<ref name=nobanis>{{cite web |url=http://www.nobanis.org/files/factsheets/Rosa_rugosa.pdf |title=NOBANIS — Invasive Alien Species Fact Sheet — ''Rosa rugosa'' |author=Weidema, I. |date=2006 |work=Online Database of the European Network on Invasive Alien Species — NOBANIS |access-date=29 August 2012}}</ref> Because of its robustness, sprouting ability, and seeds that are easily spread and may survive for years, eradication is very difficult and in countries where well-established, full eradication is considered unlikely.<ref>{{cite web| title=Rynket rose | url=https://mst.dk/natur-vand/natur/invasive-arter/hvad-kan-du-selv-goere-invasive-arter/bekaempelse-af-rynket-rose-uden-brug-af-pesticider/ | publisher=[[Ministry of Environment (Denmark)|Danish Ministry of Environment]] | access-date=1 June 2023 | archive-date=1 June 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230601064220/https://mst.dk/natur-vand/natur/invasive-arter/hvad-kan-du-selv-goere-invasive-arter/bekaempelse-af-rynket-rose-uden-brug-af-pesticider/ | url-status=dead }}</ref> The species can also be spread by birds and mammals that eat the berries.<ref name="EDDMapS">{{Cite web|url=https://www.eddmaps.org/ipane/ipanespecies/shrubs/rosa_rugosa.cfm?|title=Rosa rugosa|website=EDDMapS.org|language=en|access-date=2019-04-06}}</ref>

It is naturalized in many parts of Europe, particularly in coastal areas of northern Europe. It was first introduced into England from Japan in 1796, and then in Germany in 1845. This was the first presence of the flower within the European continent. In 1875, ''Rosa rugosa'' was found in Denmark and then in Sweden in 1918. By 2001, the flower species had become well established within 16 European countries.<ref name=Breed2004>{{Cite journal|last1=Breed|first1=Martin|last2=Wenhao Gan|last3=Isermann|first3=Maike|last4=Zhang|first4=Shuping|date=2018-04-10|title=Invasive Rosa rugosa populations outperform native populations, but some populations have greater invasive potential than others|journal=Scientific Reports|language=en|volume=8|issue=1|pages=5735|doi=10.1038/s41598-018-23974-3|doi-access=free|pmid=29636551|issn=2045-2322|pmc=5893583|bibcode=2018NatSR...8.5735Z}}</ref> Because of its invasiveness, it is illegal to sell the plant in some countries, including Denmark and Finland.<ref>{{cite web | title=Rynket rose - hyben | url=https://mst.dk/natur-vand/natur/artsleksikon/froeplanter/rynket-rose-hyben/ | publisher=[[Ministry of Environment (Denmark)|Danish Ministry of Environment]] | access-date=1 June 2023 | archive-date=1 June 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230601062825/https://mst.dk/natur-vand/natur/artsleksikon/froeplanter/rynket-rose-hyben/ | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news| title=Finland bans imports, sales of invasive rose species | url=https://yle.fi/a/3-10811231 | date=1 July 2019 | publisher=[[Yle]] | access-date=1 June 2023 }}</ref> On [[Sylt]], an island in the north of Germany, it is sufficiently abundant to have become known as the "Sylt rose".<ref name=CABI />

It is considered [[noxious weed|noxious]] in some states of the US.<ref>{{cite web |author1=USDA, NRCS. National Plant Data Team |title=Rugosa Rose |url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/factsheet/pdf/fs_roru.pdf |website=The Plants Database |publisher=USDA, NRCS |location=Greensboro, NC |date=13 May 2002}}</ref> ''R. rugosa'' was first introduced into North America in 1845. The first report of it being naturalized far from the location in which it was planted occurred on [[Nantucket]] in 1899 and was spreading rapidly by 1911. By 1920, the rose had been well established in Nantucket and in [[Connecticut]].<ref name="EDDMapS" /> Ten years later it was said to be "straying rapidly" and today it is naturalized on the entire coast of [[New England]] and in scattered locations around the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast]] and [[Pacific Northwest]].<ref name=BONAP>{{BONAP|ref|genus=Rosa|species=rugosa|access-date=27 April 2019}}</ref> ''R. rugosa'' has also become naturalized in Argentina, Australia and New Zealand.<ref name=CABI/><ref name=Breed2004/>

==Potential allergen ==
Pollen or fragrance of rose may cause an [[allergic reaction]].<ref name="Weidema-2006" />

==Vernacular names==
In [[Japanese language|Japanese]], it is called {{nihongo|''hamanasu''|浜茄子}} "beach aubergine", {{nihongo|''hamanashi''|浜梨}} "beach pear", or simply {{nihongo|"bara"|薔薇}} "rose".<ref>{{cite web|title=Flower Calendar|url=https://www.kunaicho.go.jp/e-event/hanadayori-cal.html|work=[[Imperial Household Agency]]|access-date=10 February 2020}}</ref> In [[Chinese language| Mandarin]] Chinese, it is called ''méiguì huā'' ({{lang|zh|玫瑰花}}) "rose" or ''cì méiguì'' ({{lang|zh|刺玫瑰}}) "thorned rose". In [[Korean language|Korean]], the species is called ''haedanghwa'' ({{korean|해당화}}, {{linktext|海棠|花}}), literally "flowers near the seashore".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nature.go.kr/plant/plantGuide/results/view.jsp?name_id=13169&returnUrl=%2Fplant%2FplantGuide%2Fsearch%2Fgeneral.jsp%3Fplant_name%3D%C7%D8%B4%E7%C8%AD%26size%3D10%26init_check%3DY%26start%3D1%26selLang%3DK |title=Haedanghwa (해당화) |publisher=Korea National Arboretum |language=ko |access-date=2008-08-06}} {{Dead link|date=September 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref>{{citation needed|date=May 2014}}
